strapline: Amnesty asks for the 18 to be freed before two court dates; the consortium takes the march to law; Mwitumwa's petition; Kazadi fined; Musokotwane on investors and the IMF

stories.title: 'Must immediately release the eighteen': Amnesty International asks Hichilema to free the treason detainees, ahead of High Court rulings on their liberty on 20 and 24 November
stories.excerpt: In an Urgent Action dated Tuesday 17 November, Amnesty International asked President Hakainde Hichilema to release Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others detained since the August election, saying they were held 16 days without charge, denied timely access to courts, lawyers and family, and allegedly tortured. Reported by Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer on Wednesday, the appeal lands as the High Court prepares rulings on 20 and 24 November. Spokesperson Elvis Nkandu told News Diggers the government does not control judges.

image.label: UA 121/26
image.caption: Amnesty International's Urgent Action names 18 opposition figures charged with treason on 29 August and asks for their immediate release.

body: Amnesty International has added its name to the calls for the release of the 18 men charged with treason after Zambia's 13 August general election. In an Urgent Action dated Tuesday 17 November, numbered UA 121/26 and indexed AFR 63/1686/2026, Amnesty International asked President Hakainde Hichilema to free the detainees at once, Zambia Monitor reported on Wednesday 18 November. The Zambian Observer carried the same appeal on Wednesday evening.

The document names the 18; the two reports list six of them: Ezra Tolopa, Dickson Tembo, Victor Muzyamba, Harry Valden Findlay, Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu. Amnesty describes the 18 as affiliated to the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) and the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance, and says they are being held for exercising their rights to take part in public affairs and to voice opposing political views. Zambia Monitor's account of the document says the detainees were held without charge, denied timely access to the courts, to lawyers and to their families, and allegedly tortured.

The Urgent Action, as summarised by Zambia Monitor, sets out a sequence of events. On 1 August, Tolopa, Tembo and Muzyamba were arrested at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport and, Amnesty alleges, tortured, including by waterboarding. On 9 August four men were charged with a terrorism-related offence and moved to Mwembeshi Correctional Facility. On 14 August, the day after the vote, security forces raided a property linked to Mundubile and arrested him and others; Amnesty alleges that Mutotwe Kafwaya, who was at the property, was fatally shot. Those held were, in Amnesty's account, kept for 16 days without charge. On 29 August the 18 were charged with treason, and on 30 August they were moved to Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility, where they remain.

body.text: must be exercised consistently with Zambia's obligations under international human rights law
body.attribution: Amnesty International, Urgent Action of 17 November 2026, on the authorities' powers to investigate and prosecute, as quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: Amnesty's position, as both outlets report it, is that national security cannot justify arbitrary detention or restrictions on freedom of expression and association, and that the authorities' legitimate power to investigate and prosecute genuine offences has to be used within Zambia's international obligations. The Zambian Observer quotes the document as saying the authorities "must immediately release the eighteen individuals". Neither report carried a response from the government to the appeal.

The government's general position was set out this week by Chief Government Spokesperson Elvis Nkandu. In an interview reported by News Diggers on Wednesday, Nkandu responded to Economic Front leader Wynter Kabimba, who had warned that the ruling party would suffer in the long run if the State failed to secure convictions or dropped the treason case. Nkandu said the government was law-abiding and did not control judges, and that the UPND would stay in power because of its works rather than out of sympathy.

Calls for release have also come from inside Zambian politics. Former minister George Chulumanda, responding to the police advice against the 25 November term-limit processions, called for Mundubile and Zulu to be freed and urged Zambians to defend the Constitution through peaceful action, the Zambian Observer reported on Wednesday.

The Council of Churches in Zambia has meanwhile sought to correct the narrative about its role on the day of the arrests. Its General Secretary, Rev Canon James Phiri, told a caller on Radio Christian Voice's Chat Back programme that the CCZ had been engaged as a neutral party to pass Mundubile and Zulu to their lawyers at the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, not to hand them to the State, and that church leaders only noticed police officers as the two were being escorted outside, the Zambian Observer reported, citing KBN TV. Phiri also said the current presidential term limit was appropriate.

The appeal arrives at a decisive moment for the detainees' lawyers. The Lusaka High Court is due to rule on Friday 20 November on a preliminary issue raised by the State in the separate bail application brought by Mundubile and Zulu on seditious practices charges, and on Tuesday 24 November on the constitutional bail application filed by all 18, News Diggers reported on Tuesday 17 November. Defence lawyer Sakwiba Sikota, the paper reported, described the security arrangements around the treason case as "over-dramatised".

body.confirmed: Amnesty International issued an Urgent Action dated 17 November calling for the release of the 18, as reported by Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer. The 18 were charged with treason on 29 August and are held at Mukobeko. The High Court has fixed 20 and 24 November for its rulings, per News Diggers. The government's spokesperson says it does not control judges, per News Diggers.
body.unverified: The allegations of torture, including waterboarding, and the circumstances of Mutotwe Kafwaya's death are Amnesty's account; neither report includes a government or police answer to them. No response from the government to the Urgent Action itself had been reported by Wednesday night. Charged is not guilty: all 18 are presumed innocent.

stories.title: Reasons and another date, or an appeal to the minister: the anti-third-term consortium invokes a 2014 ruling against the police advice, as a priest, an analyst and Lubinda weigh in
stories.excerpt: The civil society groups told not to march on 25 November say they will test the police advice against the 2014 LAZ v Attorney General ruling, which requires the police to give reasons and propose another date, and will appeal to the Home Affairs Minister if no date is offered by Thursday 19 November, former LAZ president Linda Kasonde said in a statement carried by the Zambian Observer. George Chulumanda called the advice 'dictatorship in uniform'; analyst Neo Simutanyi told News Diggers the UPND should groom a successor.

image.label: LAZ v AG, 2014
image.caption: The consortium defending the two-term limit says the police must give reasons and an alternative date, as a 2014 judgment requires.

body: A day after the Zambia Police Service advised both consortiums planning processions on Wednesday 25 November not to proceed, the groups defending the two-term limit have set out how they intend to answer. In a statement reported by the Zambian Observer on Wednesday 18 November, citing TV Yatu, former Law Association of Zambia president Linda Kasonde said the advice, which cited intelligence and the national security situation, amounted to a restriction of constitutional freedoms and continued a pattern of limiting public gatherings. The organisers, she said, would challenge it on legal grounds, relying on the 2014 case of LAZ v The Attorney General, in which the courts held that police who consider a demonstration unsafe must give reasons and propose an alternative date.

The statement sets a short clock. If the police do not offer an alternative date by Thursday 19 November, the organisers will appeal to the Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security, the Observer reported. The procession was notified to the police on 4 November by a consortium including Chapter One Foundation, the Zambia Council for Social Development and Transparency International Zambia, whose joint statement that day was signed by Josiah Kalala, Leah Mitaba and Maurice Nyambe, according to the Rio Times.

The minister to whom any appeal would go has already given his view. Home Affairs Minister Clement Andeleki told News Diggers he did not expect anyone to take to the streets on 25 November, for or against the limit, because President Hakainde Hichilema was not seeking a third term and was focused on development in his new five-year mandate. He urged civil society and concerned citizens to raise their concerns through established procedures rather than on the street. State House has said the campaign to remove the limit has nothing to do with the head of state, communications official Clayson Hamasaka having said this month that it began among citizens satisfied with the President's leadership, the Rio Times reported.

That answer did not satisfy George Chulumanda. The former minister, in remarks carried by the Zambian Observer on Wednesday, described the police decision as "this is dictatorship in uniform", accused the government of restricting democratic freedoms, called for the release of Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, and said Zambians must defend the Constitution through peaceful action, not violence.

body.text: A priest in Mansa, a professor in Ndola

body: The churches continued to speak. Fr Andrew Chewe Mukosa, parish priest of St Francis Kapesha Catholic Church in Mansa, said abolishing presidential term limits would be wrong and must not be allowed, that limits give different leaders a chance and set a legal boundary on how long a president rules, and that civic leaders should be spending their energy on agriculture, energy and growth instead, the Zambian Observer reported. The Observer also republished a letter of 5 November from the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia's executive director, Rev Allan Kasungami, calling for an immediate end to the debate and describing the two-term rule as a cornerstone that should not be altered for political expediency, a position the EFZ traces to the 2001 Oasis Declaration against Frederick Chiluba's third term. On Radio Christian Voice, the Council of Churches in Zambia's general secretary, Rev Canon James Phiri, said the current limit was appropriate.

body.text: You should groom a leader to take over from him. You should groom a leader to implement his programmes.
body.attribution: Dr Neo Simutanyi, political analyst, in an interview with News Diggers published on 18 November

body: From Ndola, political analyst Dr Neo Simutanyi offered the ruling party a different route out of the argument. In an interview with News Diggers he advised the UPND to start grooming President Hichilema's successor, warning that tying the Grow Zambia Agenda to one person was a risk for the programme itself.

News Diggers also reported the return to public politics of Given Lubinda, the former vice-president of the Patriotic Front. Describing himself as still a political animal, Lubinda said he was back to mobilising the opposition, that several party leaders had offered him a presidential candidacy or a running-mate slot before the August poll and that he had declined because he believed the opposition needed to unite, and that he had predicted in 2022 that a divided opposition would lose in 2026. He warned the UPND that pushing the term-limits debate could harm the party. The Rio Times noted that Lubinda has called for a referendum on the question.

Citizens petitioned the National Assembly on 27 October to abolish the limit, and no date for the House to consider the petition has been confirmed, the Rio Times reported. The police have not published the intelligence behind their advice, which does not name either consortium, nor set out any consequence for marching regardless.

stories.title: 'Housekeeper and personal assistant': former ambassador Martha Mwitumwa petitions the High Court over her treason arrest and an August 'abduction', saying she was held four days
stories.excerpt: Martha Lungu Mwitumwa, 59, formerly ambassador to Switzerland, has asked the Lusaka High Court to order her immediate release, arguing that her treason arrest this month and what she calls an abduction in August breached her constitutional rights, News Diggers and the Zambian Observer report. The petition names the Attorney General and says she was held four days in August and questioned about Brian Mundubile, for whom she says she worked only as housekeeper and personal assistant. Police charged her on 9 November with plotting to usurp executive power.

image.label: Four days in August
image.caption: The former envoy's petition asks the High Court to rule that both her arrest in November and her detention in August were unconstitutional.

body: A former ambassador charged with treason has turned to the High Court to challenge not only her arrest this month but an episode in August that her family at the time described as an abduction. Martha Lungu Mwitumwa, who served as Zambia's ambassador to Switzerland and permanent representative to the United Nations offices in Geneva and Vienna, has petitioned the Lusaka High Court for her immediate release, the Zambian Observer reported on Tuesday 17 November and News Diggers on Wednesday 18 November. The petition names the Attorney General as respondent.

According to News Diggers' report, Mwitumwa says she was held for four days in August and questioned about her ties to Brian Mundubile, the NRPUP presidential candidate who is himself detained on treason charges. The paper reports that she explained she was his housekeeper and personal assistant. The Zambian Observer's account is the same: her association with Mundubile, she says, was limited to those two roles, and she argues that both the August detention and her November arrest violated her constitutional rights.

The Zambia Police Service announced her arrest on Monday 9 November. In a statement issued by its spokesperson, Chipo Kaitisha, and reported by News Diggers that evening, the police said they had formally arrested and charged Mwitumwa, 59, with treason under section 43(1) of the Penal Code, alleging that between November 2025 and 23 October 2026, in Lusaka district, she acted with unidentified people to prepare an unlawful plan aimed at usurping the executive power of the State. No further detail of the alleged plan has been reported. She is one of several people arrested on treason-related allegations since the August election.

The August episode entered the public record through an open letter from Mwitumwa's husband to the Inspector General of Police, Graphel Musamba, published by the Zambian Observer on 10 August. The letter said that on the morning of Sunday 9 August Mwitumwa and a companion, Hanel Katontoka, left home for a church service in Libala, that Mwitumwa made a distress call saying three unmarked white vehicles were following her near the InterContinental Hotel, that shots were fired and the car was forced to stop, and that police stations across Lusaka had no record of either woman in custody. The family described both women as members of the NRPUP campaign team and said it suspected political involvement. None of those claims has been tested in court, and no police account of the August events has been reported.

body.confirmed: Mwitumwa was arrested and charged with treason on 9 November, per the police statement reported by News Diggers. She has petitioned the Lusaka High Court for release, naming the Attorney General, per News Diggers and the Zambian Observer. Her stated relationship with Mundubile is that of housekeeper and personal assistant.
body.unverified: Her account of a four-day detention and questioning in August, and her family's description of an abduction by unmarked vehicles, are allegations in a petition and an open letter; the State's response has not been reported. The substance of the alleged plan is not public. Charged is not guilty: she is presumed innocent.

stories.title: K30,000 each or nine months: David Kazadi and Mwaka Halwindi are convicted under a plea agreement in the obscene material case, as the producer apologises and cites counselling
stories.excerpt: Film producer David Kazadi, 34, and Mwaka Halwindi, 23, pleaded guilty under a plea agreement and were each fined K30,000, payable by Tuesday 1 December, with nine months' imprisonment in default, the Zambian Observer reported on Wednesday 18 November. The deal, struck under the Plea Negotiations and Agreements Act, was disclosed to Lusaka magistrate Kawama Mwamfuli on 10 November, Zambia Monitor reported. Kazadi said on Facebook that an apology alone could not undo what had happened and that he had undergone counselling, News Diggers reported.

image.label: Act No. 20 of 2010
image.caption: The case ended with a plea agreement, a tool prosecutors and the Judiciary have been promoting as an alternative to lengthy trials.

body: A case that began with three not-guilty pleas ended on Wednesday 18 November with a negotiated settlement. At the Lusaka Magistrates' Court, film producer David Kazadi, 34, and Mwaka Halwindi, 23, pleaded guilty under a plea agreement to charges relating to the production, possession and circulation of obscene material, were convicted, and were each fined K30,000, the Zambian Observer reported. The fines are payable on or before Tuesday 1 December; in default, each faces nine months' imprisonment.

The State's allegation, as the Observer summarised it, was that between 1 January 2023 and 30 June 2025 Kazadi circulated videos involving Halwindi and shared other explicit material over WhatsApp. A third accused, Ruby Muzandu, 23, was charged alongside them; the Observer's report records no plea, conviction or sentence in her case.

The plea agreement was struck under the Plea Negotiations and Agreements Act No. 20 of 2010. Zambia Monitor reported on 10 November that when the matter came before Magistrate Kawama Mwamfuli for the start of trial that day, Senior Public Prosecutor Judith Mauka and Public Prosecutor Hope Mikwala disclosed that the State had reached an agreement with the three accused, but that it had not yet been served on the defence or filed. The magistrate ordered it served and filed by close of business and adjourned the case to 18 November. An earlier trial date in September had been lost because the magistrate was sitting on election petition tribunals, the Monitor reported.

The Monitor placed the deal in a wider context: the National Prosecution Authority, the Law Association of Zambia, the Legal Aid Board and the Judiciary have been promoting plea bargaining as an alternative to lengthy trials, visiting Chimbokaila and Mwembeshi correctional facilities to explain the process to remandees. The Act has been on the books since 2010 but is little used. Any agreement remains subject to the court, which must satisfy itself that the accused is pleading guilty to an offence the facts support and that the deal serves the interests of justice.

Ahead of the hearing, Kazadi addressed the public. In a statement on his Facebook page reported by News Diggers on Wednesday, he apologised over the controversy that led to the case, acknowledged that an apology alone could not undo what had happened, and said he had undergone counselling and was committed to becoming a better person.

body.confirmed: Kazadi and Halwindi were convicted and fined K30,000 each under a plea agreement, payable by 1 December with nine months' imprisonment in default, per the Zambian Observer. The agreement was disclosed in court on 10 November before Magistrate Kawama Mwamfuli, per Zambia Monitor. Kazadi apologised on Facebook, per News Diggers.
body.unverified: The outcome for Ruby Muzandu is not stated in the Observer's report. The terms of the agreement beyond the fines have not been published.

stories.title: 'We are scared of foreign investments': in Kitwe, Musokotwane says fear of outside capital holds Africa back, and defends the IMF as a US$1.47 billion deal awaits approval
stories.excerpt: At the Copperbelt 2027 National Budget Symposium in Kitwe, Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane said that China, Japan and Germany grew by opening up to foreign investment and that investors create jobs for local firms rather than crowding them out, News Diggers reported on Wednesday 18 November. The Zambian Observer reported him saying mineral wealth is no reason to leave the IMF, whose 191 members include Saudi Arabia, after Zambia's US$1.7 billion facility closed in January and a new US$1.472 billion arrangement reached staff level in October.

image.label: 191 members
image.caption: The finance minister took the 2027 budget to the Copperbelt and used the platform to answer two of its loudest critics: those wary of foreign investors and those wary of the IMF.

body: Finance and National Planning Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane took the 2027 budget to the Copperbelt this week and used the occasion to confront a strain of economic nationalism he thinks is costing the continent. Speaking at the Copperbelt 2027 National Budget Symposium in Kitwe, he said that one of the reasons Africa lags other regions is a fear of foreign investment, News Diggers reported on Wednesday 18 November.

body.text: One of the reasons Africa is lagging behind is because we are scared of foreign investments.
body.attribution: Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane, Minister of Finance and National Planning, at the Copperbelt 2027 National Budget Symposium in Kitwe, as reported by News Diggers on 18 November

body: His argument, as the paper reported it, was historical: China, Japan and Germany all grew by opening their economies to outside capital at a time when they lacked enough of their own. He rejected the view that foreign investors damage local business, saying they create jobs and opportunities for local entrepreneurs. The theme runs through the 2027 budget itself, which Zambia Monitor reported on 7 November sets a copper production target of 930,000 tonnes for next year on the road to three million tonnes a year by 2031, leaning on expansions at First Quantum, Barrick Lumwana, Konkola and Mopani and on the greenfield Kitumba and KoBold projects, with a promise of a stable and predictable mining tax regime.

The minister also answered the argument that a copper-rich country has no business with the International Monetary Fund. In remarks carried by the Zambian Observer on Wednesday, he said the IMF has 191 members, including the world's largest economies and major oil producers, and pointed to Saudi Arabia, whose finance minister, Mohammed Aljadaan, chairs the Fund's International Monetary and Financial Committee. Zambia completed the final review of its Extended Credit Facility in January 2026, with cumulative disbursements of about US$1.7 billion, and in October reached a staff-level agreement on a new 36-month arrangement of about US$1.472 billion, which still needs the approval of the IMF board. He tied the approach to the 2027 budget and the Grow Zambia Agenda, summarising it as "partnerships where necessary, national ownership always, and development benefits for all".

The same week, Mines Minister Brenda Tambatamba told a breakfast meeting with stakeholders on Tuesday that anti-corruption measures would be non-negotiable standards in her ministry as it pursued the three-million-tonne target, and that government would work with mining companies, investors, communities and civil society on illegal mining and pollution, News Diggers reported. "As a ministry, we realise that we cannot effect the much-needed change alone," the paper quoted her as saying.

Not every minister's emphasis was on openness. Industry Minister Noel Nkhoma, receiving the Zambia Development Agency's director general Albert Halwampa, called for an industrialisation master plan and a master plan for the Lobito Corridor, and warned that dumping was eroding local manufacturers' market share, Zambia Monitor reported on Tuesday 17 November. "We need to capacitate and protect our industries because that is where the jobs and budget support are coming from," he said. Halwampa suggested using World Trade Organisation mechanisms against unfair trade rather than working in isolation.

stories.title: 'Not conditional on any commercial agreements': US Democrats plan probes into Africa minerals deals from January, with the reported threat to Zambia's HIV aid at the centre
stories.excerpt: Democrats preparing to take control of the US House of Representatives in January say they will open formal investigations into the Trump administration's critical-minerals agreements in Africa, Semafor reported, in a story that reached Zambian readers through the Zambian Observer on Wednesday 18 November. Among their grievances is a March report that the State Department threatened to withhold HIV assistance to push Zambia into a minerals deal. A State Department spokesperson said US health assistance is not conditional on any commercial agreement.

image.label: Medicine and minerals
image.caption: An allegation first reported in March, that HIV aid was used as leverage in minerals talks with Zambia, is heading for congressional scrutiny.

body: The question of whether American health money was used as a bargaining chip in talks over Zambia's minerals is about to get a formal hearing in Washington. Democratic members of the US House of Representatives, who take the majority in January, intend to open investigations into the Trump administration's critical-minerals agreements across Africa, Semafor reported on Monday 16 November in a story syndicated by Yahoo News. The Zambian Observer carried the report on Wednesday 18 November, framing it around what it called the Zambia health aid controversy.

Representative Jonathan Jackson, a Democrat from Illinois, told Semafor that the deals had been struck in near-total secrecy and that his party now had a mandate to open formal investigations and commission public reports mapping who was receiving them. Jackson, Representative Linda Sánchez and Representative Jared Huffman, both of California, wrote to four federal agencies in August; Jackson said the administration's reply dodged almost all of their questions, and Sánchez called it little more than something artificial intelligence would write, adding that oversight changes in January.

The Zambian strand dates from March 2026, when the New York Times reported that the State Department had threatened to withhold HIV aid to press Zambia into a minerals agreement. Representative Jimmy Panetta, also of California, who has pressed Secretary of State Marco Rubio for details of new global health agreements signed with 36 countries, told Semafor that using lifesaving aid to extract unrelated economic concessions was what Russia, Iran or China had traditionally done. The Semafor report gives no figures for the aid at stake and names no Zambian officials or companies.

The State Department rejected the premise. A spokesperson told Semafor that "our health assistance is not conditional on any commercial agreements", and that the health pacts contained nothing related to critical minerals. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the President was willing to work with anyone to deliver for Americans, and that Democrats pursuing what she called sham investigations would be working against the American people.

For Zambia the stakes sit on both sides of the ledger: the HIV assistance the March report said was at risk, and the copper and cobalt that the Observer's report describes as the object of Washington's effort to expand access to Africa's strategic minerals. No Zambian government response to the planned probes had been reported by Wednesday night, and neither article identifies which agreement with Zambia, if any, would be examined first.

stories.title: Thirty-five boys, twenty places and a group with Zimbabwe and Eswatini: Chris Kaunda opens the under-17 camp for Maputo, as Fashion Sakala's parting shot at bloggers resurfaces
stories.excerpt: Under-17 coach Chris Kaunda has called 35 players into camp in Lusaka ahead of the CAF Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations COSAFA qualifier in Maputo from 4 to 13 December, where Zambia are drawn with Zimbabwe and Eswatini in Group C and only three COSAFA sides reach the finals in Morocco, ZamFoot and News Diggers report. The squad, including two under-15 strikers who helped win Tier B of the FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku, will be cut to 20. A file video of Fashion Sakala saying bloggers turned on him when he refused to pay them is circulating.

image.label: Group C, Maputo
image.caption: Zambia's under-17s face Zimbabwe and Eswatini in Maputo in December, with three COSAFA places at the 2027 finals in Morocco.

body: Zambia's next age-group campaign began in Lusaka on Tuesday 17 November, when 35 players reported to under-17 coach Chris Kaunda ahead of the TotalEnergies CAF Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations 2027 COSAFA qualifier, ZamFoot reported on Tuesday and News Diggers on Wednesday. The tournament runs in Maputo, Mozambique, from 4 to 13 December as part of the AUSC Region 5 Games, and Zambia have been drawn in Group C with Zimbabwe and Eswatini. Only three COSAFA teams qualify for the continental finals, which Morocco will host. Kaunda will trim the provisional squad to 20.

The list, published by ZamFoot, carries four goalkeepers, five defenders, 12 midfielders and 14 forwards, drawn mostly from academies and lower-league clubs across the country, with two boys based abroad: defender Joseph Sipilingo of Highlands Park in South Africa and forward Nathaniel Mubanga of Brooke House Academy in England. The names that caught ZamFoot's eye were two strikers promoted from the under-15s, Maxen Msimuko of Young Crocs and Samuel Musonda of Sporting Lusaka, who were central to Zambia's Tier B title at the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku, Azerbaijan, last month.

body: The senior team's week has been dominated by Fashion Sakala's retirement from international football, announced on Facebook on Tuesday, days after the 1–1 draw with Burundi. ZamFoot recorded his farewell: after much reflection he had decided to retire, representing Zambia and captaining the Chipolopolo were among the proudest moments of his life, and he would cheer for Zambia with the same pride for the rest of it. He leaves with 41 senior appearances, 12 goals and five assists, a 2017 Africa Under-20 title, goals against Portugal, Iran and Germany at that year's Under-20 World Cup and a hat-trick against Mauritania in 2021, by ZamFoot's count.

On Wednesday the Zambian Observer reported that an older video of the 29-year-old forward had resurfaced on social media, in which he says that because he refused to pay bloggers and analysts they started to write bad things about him, and that he would not change who he is. The Observer does not say when or where the clip was recorded, and it presents the remarks as Sakala's own claims, without a response from those he refers to. The Football Association of Zambia has said the door remains open should he reconsider, the Observer reported.

stories.title: K2 million from KCM for the Ngoma Awards on 10 December, and Yo Maps everywhere at the Kwacha Music Awards on 27 November: Zambia's two big nights of the year take shape
stories.excerpt: Konkola Copper Mines has put K2 million into the 2026 Ngoma Awards, the National Arts Council's flagship honours since 1997, to be handed out on 10 December, Zambian Music Blog reported on Wednesday 18 November; Culture and Arts Minister Christopher Chibuye called it an important show of support for the arts. Two weeks earlier, on Friday 27 November, the 8th Sun FM Kwacha Music Awards fill the Mulungushi International Conference Centre, with Yo Maps carrying 13 nominations and Chile One, Chef 187, Mampi and Sampa the Great in the main categories.

image.label: 27 November, 10 December
image.caption: The Kwacha Music Awards and the Ngoma Awards fall within a fortnight of each other at the end of 2026.

body: Zambia's awards season now has its dates and its money. Konkola Copper Mines has contributed K2 million to the 2026 Ngoma Awards, Zambian Music Blog reported on Wednesday 18 November, at a sponsor unveiling attended by musicians, actors and content creators. Culture and Arts Minister Christopher Chibuye commended the mining company for what he described as an important show of support for the country's arts sector and for investing in an event that celebrates Zambian creatives. The ceremony is scheduled for Thursday 10 December; a venue has not been announced.

The Ngoma Awards, established in 1997 and organised by the National Arts Council of Zambia, are the country's flagship national honours, spanning music, dance, theatre, visual arts, creative writing, media arts, fashion and comedy. KCM joins a sponsor list that includes the Wonderful Group of Companies, NAPSA, Quorum, UNICAF University and Capstone TV, the blog reported.

Before that, the music industry gathers for its own night. The 8th Sun FM Kwacha Music Awards take place on Friday 27 November at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre in Lusaka, with the red carpet from 18:00 and the ceremony from 19:00, according to the nominations list Zambian Music Blog published on 6 October. Yo Maps leads the field with 13 nominations, including Best Artist (Male), Song of the Year for both "Hello" and "It's Over" with Makadzi, and Album of the Year for "Vibes on Vibes".

He is up against a crowded field. Best Artist (Male) also lists 76 Drums, Chef 187, Chile One, Dizmo, Drimz, Pompi and T-Sean; Best Artist (Female) runs from Mampi and Towela Kaira to Sampa the Great, Xaven, Bombshell Grenade, Medoreen Besa, Rockstone and Tianna. Chile One's "Destiny", T-Sean's "Still Waters", Tio Nason's "God Sound", Petersen's "So Cha Cha Toa", Mag44's "The Way" and Kayz Adams's "Witina" contest Album of the Year alongside Yo Maps, while Song of the Year includes Slapdee and Dizmo's "Asante", Chile One's "Ba Neighbor" and Vinchenzo and Towela Kaira's "My Man My Man". The newcomer categories introduce Boy Kay, Dreckzine and Mwana Kalampa among the men and Kunda, Nyarai and Tina Selemani among the women.

Between the two ceremonies falls the release calendar that will shape next year's lists: Rich Bizzy's 23-track "Africa" and Jae Cash's second album "Chawama Johnhaward" both appear on the blog's latest releases, alongside a new Kanina Kandalama video, "Wiya", with JZyNo.

analysis.title: An Urgent Action changes the audience, not the law
analysis.body: Amnesty International's appeal does not bind anyone. Urgent Actions are letters to a government and a call to members to write their own; their force is reputational, and governments routinely answer that the matter is before the courts. That answer is available here, because it is true: the High Court rules on Friday on whether the State's preliminary objection blocks the sedition bail application, and on Tuesday on constitutional bail for all 18. What the Amnesty document does is widen the audience for those two rulings, from Lusaka to the diplomatic missions and lenders who read Amnesty's index numbers. It also fixes a version of the August timeline on the record, including allegations of torture and of a death during the 14 August raid, which the State has not publicly answered. The strongest case for the government is the one Elvis Nkandu made: it does not control judges, and the charges will be tested in court. The strongest case against it is Amnesty's: 16 days without charge is not a matter for a judge to cure later. What to watch is less the rulings themselves than their reasoning, and whether any ministry replies to UA 121/26 at all.

analysis.title: The 2014 judgment gives the consortium a procedure, not a march
analysis.body: The anti-third-term consortium has chosen the one line of attack the police statement left open. LAZ v The Attorney General, decided in 2014, is read by the organisers as requiring the police, when they judge a procession unsafe, to say why and to offer another date. Tuesday's statement did neither: it cited intelligence it did not describe and proposed no alternative. If no date arrives by Thursday the groups say they will appeal to the Home Affairs Minister, who has already said he expects nobody to march because there is no third-term bid to march against. That sets up the next question: whether the matter goes to court before 25 November, and whether a court will order the police to do what the consortium says the 2014 ruling requires. The government's position is coherent on its own terms: the President is not a candidate, petitions are a citizen's right, and the police are the judge of security. The organisers' position is equally coherent: the right to assemble is not conditional on the cause being necessary. Neither side has yet said what happens if people walk anyway.

analysis.title: Musokotwane's two defences are really one argument
analysis.body: In Kitwe the finance minister argued for foreign investors; in the same news cycle he argued for the IMF. They are the same case made to two different audiences. The Copperbelt hears the investor argument as a defence of the mining houses whose expansions carry the 930,000-tonne target for 2027 and the three-million-tonne ambition for 2031. The national audience hears the IMF argument as a defence of a second programme, US$1.472 billion over 36 months, agreed at staff level in October and still awaiting the board. What links them is the minister's view that Zambia lacks capital and should borrow credibility where it can, citing China, Japan and Germany on one hand and Saudi Arabia's seat at the IMF's top table on the other. The counter-arguments are familiar and not frivolous: that investor-friendly terms have in the past cost the Treasury revenue, and that Fund programmes carry conditions on spending and tax whose weight tends to fall on households before it falls on mines. The test will be the board date for the new arrangement and whether the 2027 budget's mining tax promises survive the first copper price dip.
